name: Red ochre body painting

lead: Red ochre body painting is the use of red iron-oxide clay pigment on the skin and hair. It gives a red-orange tint and a glossy, textured finish, and has been used as adornment and for sun and insect protection in many cultures.

Processing of red ochre is dated to around 300,000 years ago, and ochre appears in burials, cave art and cosmetic traditions from the Himba, Maasai, Māori, Aboriginal Australians and ancient Egyptians.

paras: Traditional preparations mix ochre with animal fat, fish oil or plant oils and apply it to skin and hair; the Himba otjize combines butterfat and ochre, sometimes perfumed with resin.
Ochres are described as non-toxic, though that is marked as needing a citation on Wikipedia. Some historical pigments such as orpiment were highly toxic because of arsenic.

chain: Red-orange tint and styled appearance, with sun and insect protection
angle.text: The paste colours and styles skin and hair, as in Himba otjize. Cultures have used it for beauty and for practical protection.

lead: Red ochre body painting is the application of ochre, a clay earth pigment coloured by iron oxides (red ochre by hematite), to the skin and hair.[1] It is typically mixed with fat or oil.[1]

It improves appearance by giving a deep red-orange colour and a distinctive style. Among Himba women, otjize, a paste of butterfat and ochre, is considered a highly desirable beauty cosmetic, and it also cleanses during long periods without water and deters insects.[2] A 2022 study explored Himba knowledge as inspiration for iron-oxide UV-blocking nanocosmetics.[3]

Archaeologists date processing of red ochre to about 300,000 years ago, with use by early Neandertals reported and engraved ochre at Blombos Cave around 75,000 years ago, though body use for the earliest dates is not specified.[1][4][5]
infobox: Animal fat, fish oil, plant oils[1]

paras: Ochres are clay pigments made mainly of iron oxides with varying clay and sand. Body preparations typically combine ochre with fats or oils.[1]

Wikipedia lists red ochre use at Blombos Cave (~75,000 years), Mungo Man (burial sprinkled with ochre), the Red Lady of Paviland (~33,000 years), and a hand image at Pech Merle (~25,000 years).[1] Studies report ochre use by early Neandertals, engraved ochre at Blombos, and ochre and shells at Qafzeh Cave, Israel.[4][5][6]

Among living traditions, Himba women colour skin and braids with ochre and fat; Maasai use ochre similarly; Māori kōkōwai was mixed with fish or shark oil, said to repel sandflies; Aboriginal Australians use it for ceremony, decoration and sun protection; Ancient Egyptians used red ochre as rouge or lip colour.[1][2]

Himba otjize is a butterfat and ochre paste, often perfumed with omuzumba shrub resin, symbolising earth's red colour and blood as life's essence. Married women or mothers wear the Erembe headpiece with braids coloured with otjize.[2]
No studies found. A 2022 paper on Himba-inspired iron-oxide UV-blocking nanocosmetics is laboratory work on engineered materials.[3]
